profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab two weeks before a submission deadline for a workshop follow-up paper on Equilibriated Recurrent Neural Networks (ERNNs). The team has reproduced the main ERNN architecture on long-sequence benchmarks, but their latest training runs show unstable behavior: some seeds converge quickly while others stall, memory usage is unexpectedly high, and the claimed 3-10x speedup is not appearing in the internal benchmark report. The agenda is to diagnose why the current implementation is not matching expected stability and efficiency, decide what the likely root cause is, and agree on a concrete fix to test that day. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan for a 'stability fix' and a rerun of the benchmark suite before the next lab review.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: sequence modeling, dynamical systems interpretations of neural networks, empirical benchmarking
members.background: Maya leads the lab's recurrent modeling efforts and previously worked on implicit layers and neural ODE-style architectures in industry research.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve the paper's core claim that ERNNs are both stable and computationally efficient, and is worried that the current issue will undermine the speedup narrative if the implementation turns out to require expensive inner iterations.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the ERNN 'converges,' they usually mean the hidden-state fixed-point iteration settles within a small residual tolerance at each time step, because that is the mechanism guaranteeing stable dynamics.

The 'benchmark run' refers to the curated long-sequence reproduction suite on permuted sequential MNIST and character-level PTB with the standard 200-step truncation and warm-started hidden-state solver settings used in prior lab reports.

A 'stability fix' should be local to the recurrent update and not include changing training instrumentation, logging, or memory-saving machinery, which are implementation details rather than model behavior.
If the implementation matches the intended equilibrium-manifold update, backpropagation cost should be roughly comparable to vanilla RNNs aside from a small bounded inner-solver overhead.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: PyTorch internals, training efficiency, distributed experimentation, profiling and memory debugging
members.background: Leo maintains the lab's experiment framework and recently ported the ERNN codepath into the shared training stack used for all sequence models.
members.private_state: He wants a fix that makes the runs reliable inside the shared framework without introducing one-off code, and is concerned that the issue may actually be due to autograd graph retention and benchmark methodology rather than the recurrent dynamics themselves.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the model 'converges,' they usually mean end-to-end training loss and validation accuracy become reproducible across seeds, not that every hidden-state inner iteration reaches a strict residual threshold.

The 'benchmark run' means the standard cluster throughput job on the shared stack, which uses full-length sequences where available, mixed precision, and the framework's default profiling hooks so comparisons across models are apples-to-apples.

A 'stability fix' naturally includes changes to checkpointing, detach boundaries, and solver implementation details if those remove graph blow-up or numerical issues, because those are part of the actual training system.
If ERNN needs multiple fixed-point iterations, the only fair speed claim is wall-clock throughput under the shared profiling setup, even if theoretical per-step costs look similar.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the ERNN update is 'converging' or 'not converging.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the per-time-step hidden-state solver reaches a stable fixed point with a sufficiently small residual, indicating the equilibrium-manifold update is behaving correctly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the full training run becomes stable across epochs and seeds, with loss no longer oscillating or diverging.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML troubleshooting, 'convergence' is commonly used for both inner numerical convergence and outer training convergence, and each interpretation fits the observed symptoms well enough that neither participant feels the need to disambiguate.

misalignment_points.topic: Which benchmark run they are diagnosing
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the benchmark run from yesterday' and 'the speedup numbers.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the lab's reproduction notebook results on the curated ERNN suite, especially the warm-started pMNIST/PTB runs with truncated BPTT and minimal logging.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the shared-framework cluster benchmark job that used full framework defaults, profiler hooks, and in one case full sequence unrolling.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both runs were launched the same day, discussed in the same Slack thread, and summarized as 'yesterday's benchmark,' so the label feels uniquely identifying even though it refers to different artifacts.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree they need a 'stability fix' before rerunning experiments.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means adjusting the ERNN recurrent update itself, such as damping, residual tolerance, or warm-start behavior, while leaving the broader training stack untouched.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes autograd detach points, activation checkpointing, fused solver code, and other systems-level changes that affect whether the model trains robustly in practice.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both model-level and systems-level changes plausibly belong under the broad phrase 'stability fix,' and in troubleshooting meetings teams often intentionally speak at that level without enumerating scope boundaries.

misalignment_points.topic: How they will 'rerun with the standard setup'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to rerun the model with the 'standard setup' after the fix.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes 'standard setup' means the lab's paper-reproduction configuration: 200-step truncated BPTT, warm-started fixed-point iteration from the previous hidden state, and profiler disabled.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes 'standard setup' means the shared training template: framework-default sequence handling, mixed precision on, profiler hooks enabled for throughput accounting, and the generic solver wrapper.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each person has a well-established local notion of 'standard setup' from their own responsibilities, and because both are established defaults rather than explicit design choices, neither thinks to restate them.
